sentences.text: Citipati was among the largest members of its group, with adults reaching lengths between 2.5 and 2.9 meters and weighing from 75 to 110 kilograms.

This large-bodied theropod possessed an unusually long neck and a shortened tail, features that contrasted with most other carnivorous dinosaurs. Its head was small and highly pneumatized, ending in a stout, toothless beak made of horn.
The eggs laid by this dinosaur are the longest known definitive oviraptorid eggs, measuring exactly 18 centimeters in length.
Remarkably, a specific individual survived a healed injury to its ulna bone while still incubating its nest.
Citipati is one of the best-known oviraptorids because of the many well-preserved skeletons found, including several sitting on nests with eggs.
Remains of this animal were first collected in the 1990s at the Ukhaa Tolgod locality within the Djadokhta Formation.

A small fossilized embryo was discovered in 1993 during a joint expedition, and in 2001 James M. Clark, Mark A. Norell, and Rinchen Barsbold named the species Citipati osmolskae based on this and other specimens.
The famous specimen known as 'Big Momma' was found in 1995, described in 1999, and officially assigned to the genus in 2001.
Another specimen, catalogued as IGM 100/1004, was discovered in 1995 but was not formally referred to Citipati osmolskae until 2018.
Long feathers on its arms and tail may have served to protect eggs and young from the elements.
Nesting specimens were found sitting on top of egg clutches with limbs spread symmetrically and front limbs covering the nest perimeter.
Citipati likely fed on tougher vegetation than other herbivorous theropods found in its environment.
A 2022 study estimated the bite force of this animal to be between 349.3 N and 499.0 N.
Juvenile troodontid remains found in a nest suggest that adults might have brought prey to feed their young, hinting at an omnivorous diet.
In 2020, Gregory F. Funston and colleagues established the new subfamily Citipatiinae to separate Citipati from Oviraptor.
Citipati lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.
It inhabited arid to semiarid environments consisting of large sand dunes and short-lived water bodies.
The recorded time range for this taxon extends from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Researchers debated whether remains from the nearby Zamyn Khondt locality represent a second species of Citipati.
It is also debated whether juvenile troodontid skulls found near Citipati nests were prey, nest raiders, or evidence of nest parasitism.
Finally, it is debated whether the IGN specimen represents a second species of Citipati or a completely distinct genus.
